planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Harris's air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.

directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Harris's air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. Densely packed, curving, silvery-white leaves covered in fine trichome scales give this compact rosette an almost fuzzy, ghostly pale appearance, brightening to a soft blush pink at the base when the plant is ready to flower, with a spike of violet blossoms emerging from red bracts at maturity. Native to dry oak and pine forests of Guatemala and Honduras at higher elevations, it tolerates brighter light and slightly cooler, drier conditions than many rainforest tillandsias, reflecting its more open, seasonally dry native habitat. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times weekly, shake off excess water to prevent rot at the base, and provide bright light for the best silvery color.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with excellent air circulation; Snowball air plant is adapted to arid conditions and needs much lighter, less frequent misting than most tillandsias to avoid rot.

directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with excellent air circulation; Snowball air plant is adapted to arid conditions and needs much lighter, less frequent misting than most tillandsias to avoid rot. Slender, curling leaves are so densely coated in thick, woolly, silvery-white trichomes that the entire plant appears to be covered in a soft blanket of snow, one of the fuzziest and most visually striking of all commonly grown air plants and a favorite for terrarium and driftwood displays. Native to high-elevation, fog-fed cliffs and dry Andean slopes in Ecuador and Peru, it absorbs most of its moisture from humid air and fog rather than rainfall, making it more prone to rot from overwatering than nearly any other air plant in cultivation. Mist lightly only once or twice a week rather than soaking, ensure the plant dries completely and quickly afterward, and provide bright light and strong air movement to replicate its native high-altitude habitat.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Curly Slim air plant curls its leaves tighter when kept on the drier side and relaxes them when well hydrated, so drying thoroughly between waterings encourages its signature curl.

directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Curly Slim air plant curls its leaves tighter when kept on the drier side and relaxes them when well hydrated, so drying thoroughly between waterings encourages its signature curl. Broad, bulbous leaves twist and curl dramatically into loose ringlets, giving this popular air plant a whimsical, almost cartoonish silhouette that has made it one of the most recognizable and widely sold tillandsia species, with a tall spike of pink bracts and violet-blue flowers appearing at maturity. Native to seasonally dry forests from Mexico to Central America, it naturally sheds moisture quickly between the infrequent rains of its dry-season habitat, and its curl relaxes noticeably after a good soak before tightening again as it dries. Soak thoroughly once or twice a week and shake off excess water from the curled leaf bases, where trapped moisture is the most common cause of rot.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Snake air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.

directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Snake air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. A bulbous base tapers into long, slender, snaking leaves marked with irregular purplish-maroon speckles and blotches over green, an unusual mottled pattern combined with the plant's writhing, serpentine form that gives it its common name, topped with a spike of purple flowers emerging from pink bracts at maturity. Native to humid forests from Mexico through Central America, it prefers slightly more shade and humidity than desert-adapted tillandsia species, thriving mounted in a shaded, humid spot such as a covered porch or bathroom window. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times weekly, ensure good air circulation to dry the base fully afterward, and avoid direct hot sun, which can scorch the mottled leaves.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Ruby Glow peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Ruby Glow peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, boat-shaped, semi-succulent leaves are deep glossy green on top with a translucent window-like keel that glows a vivid ruby-red on the underside when backlit, an unusual two-tone leaf effect best displayed at eye level where light can pass through the leaves. Native to dry rock crevices in Ecuador, it is a semi-succulent species that tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil, making it a low-maintenance choice for a bright windowsill among a succulent or peperomia collection. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the deepest ruby coloring, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Happy Bean peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Happy Bean peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, curved, bean-shaped, semi-succulent leaves are densely packed along upright, fleshy stems in a distinctive pincushion arrangement, giving the plant a quirky, playful texture unlike the flatter or rounder leaves of most peperomia species. Native to dry rocky habitats in Peru, it stores water in its thick leaves and tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil, making it a good low-maintenance choice for a bright windowsill or succulent-style dish garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light to keep growth compact rather than stretched, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Prayer peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Prayer peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, folded, translucent-green leaves are shaped like tiny curved trumpets or canoes, held upright along fleshy stems in a form so distinctive it is instantly recognizable among succulent-leaved peperomias, with a pale window-like stripe running down each folded leaf that lets light filter into the plant's interior. Native to dry rocky slopes in Peru, this fully succulent species tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil and is prone to rot if kept constantly moist, making a gritty, fast-draining mix and cautious watering essential. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-formed growth, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Painted Lady philodendron holds its bright lime and yellow coloring best with strong, consistent indirect light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Painted Lady philodendron holds its bright lime and yellow coloring best with strong, consistent indirect light. Glossy, heart-shaped leaves emerge a bright chartreuse-yellow speckled and streaked with darker green flecks, a lively, sunny leaf coloring that brightens a shaded corner far more than the deep greens typical of most climbing philodendrons, with the mottled pattern varying somewhat from leaf to leaf. A vigorous climber, it develops larger, more vividly patterned leaves when trained up a moss pole rather than left to trail, and its bright color makes an eye-catching contrast against darker-leaved houseplant companions. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the vivid yellow-green coloring, keep humidity moderate to high, and water when the top inch of potting mix has dried.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
